paper_title: InfiniSplat v2: Analyzing and Improving Feed-Forward 3DGS from Any Views

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction builds 3D scenes directly from input images for novel view rendering, but learning Gaussian attributes from predicted geometry for high-quality rendering under large viewpoint changes remains challenging. We analyze limitations in Gaussian attribute learning and introduce InfiniSplat v2, which improves rendering quality through architectural and training changes. Our method decouples geometry and attribute prediction with a frozen geometry branch, aligns predicted Gaussians using ground-truth camera poses during training, and adopts large-angle target view supervision. Across six datasets, the feed-forward outputs of the same trained model achieve state-of-the-art mean LPIPS and DISTS among the evaluated methods in both pose-conditioned and pose-free settings. In the pose-conditioned setting, mean LPIPS and DISTS decrease by 25.8% and 32.9%, respectively, compared with the strongest evaluated baselines. We further find that opacity learned with only image reconstruction supervision suppresses geometrically inconsistent points. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/InfiniSplat2/

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Image-based 3D scene reconstruction aims to recover renderable 3D scene from input images to support novel view rendering for applications such as simulation, content creation, and autonomous driving. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al., 2023) enables efficient rendering through an explicit scene representation. Building on this representation, recent feed-forward methods (Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025b) directly predict Gaussian scenes from input images, eliminating the need for per-scene representation optimization at inference time. Pretrained multi-view geometry models (Wang et al., 2024; Leroy et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026d) provide useful starting point for constructing renderable scenes from images. They predict depth maps and cameras for each input view. Backprojecting these depth maps with the corresponding camera estimates into common coordinate frame yields predicted point cloud. This point cloud captures coherent scene geometry overall, but typically also contains spatially isolated clusters or clusters that are inconsistent across views. Such issues become particularly apparent after 3D aggregation, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Existing feed-forward methods (Lin et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026) combine geometry prediction from multiple views with Gaussian attribute prediction to construct renderable scenes from input images. For example, DA3-GS (Lin et al., 2025) learns Gaussian attributes on top of the geometry predicted by DA3. However, as shown in Figs. 3 and 4, renderings from DA3-GS and the other evaluated methods still exhibit blur, ghosting, and missing detail. Our work focuses on using these imperfect geometry predictions to construct Gaussian scenes that support high-quality novel view rendering. As shown in Fig. 1, InfiniSplat v2 reconstructs Gaussian scenes from predicted multi-view geometry and supports high-quality novel-view rendering at extreme viewpoints. We identify key factors that affect Gaussian learning and introduce three corresponding architectural and training improvements. First, we investigate why prior methods struggle to eliminate flying-point artifacts and find that jointly optimizing geometry and Gaussian attributes leads to geometric degradation. We therefore redesign the architecture to decouple geometry prediction from Gaussian attribute prediction while keeping the geometry branch frozen. Second, we find that using predicted camera poses during training (Lin et al., 2025) introduces pose errors. Under large-angle supervision, these errors can misguide the network during training. We therefore use GT camera poses to align the predicted Gaussians. Third, inspired by InfiniSplats strong performance under large viewpoint changes (Wang et al., 2026b), we introduce large-angle target view supervision for feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction from arbitrary input views. Our experiments show that these three improvements enhance novel view rendering quality under large viewpoint changes, even when the predicted point clouds contain numerous outliers. We evaluate the same trained model on six datasets, both with and without camera pose inputs. Our method achieves the lowest mean LPIPS and DISTS across the six datasets among the evaluated baselines in both settings. With camera pose inputs, our feed-forward reconstruction reduces LPIPS and DISTS by 25.8% and 32.9%, respectively, relative to the strongest evaluated baseline for each metric. Additionally, we find that, with only image reconstruction supervision, the trainable attribute branch learns to assign lower opacity to outliers that are geometrically inconsistent across views. These points consequently contribute less to the rendered images, reducing visible artifacts in novel views  (Fig. 7)  . Our contributions are threefold: We introduce InfiniSplat v2, feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction method for arbitrary input views. It freezes the geometry branch to decouple geometry prediction from Gaussian attribute prediction, aligns predicted Gaussians using GT camera poses during training, and adopts large-angle target view supervision. We evaluate the method on six datasets in both pose-conditioned and pose-free settings. The feed-forward outputs of the same trained model achieve the lowest mean LPIPS and DISTS among the evaluated baselines in both settings. We find that opacity learned with only image reconstruction supervision selectively suppresses the rendering contributions of geometrically inconsistent points across views. 2 Figure 2: Training pipeline of InfiniSplat v2s feed-forward reconstructor. frozen geometry branch predicts depth and cameras, while trainable branch predicts Gaussian attributes. Scale-aligned GT cameras construct the point cloud; after opacity pruning, input and large-angle target views supervise Gaussian learning.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: 2.1 FEED-FORWARD 3D GEOMETRY ESTIMATION Geometry foundation models recover scene structure from images and provide geometric basis for feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction. DUSt3R (Wang et al., 2024), MASt3R (Leroy et al., 2024), VGGT (Wang et al., 2025a), Fast3R (Yang et al., 2025), and π3 (Wang et al., 2026d) advance learned geometric reconstruction. Depth Anything 3 (DA3) (Lin et al., 2025) reconstructs geometry from varying numbers of images, with or without supplied poses. VGGT-Long (Deng et al., 2025), VGG-T3 (Elflein et al., 2026), and Scal3R (Xie et al., 2026) extend learned reconstruction to longer sequences and larger scenes. These predictions provide useful starting point, but constructing renderable Gaussian scenes also requires learning attributes such as opacity, scale, and appearance. 2.2 FEED-FORWARD GAUSSIAN SPLATTING Generalizable view synthesis learns to predict novel views or renderable representations across scenes (Wang et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2024). Feed-forward Gaussian methods pursue this goal by directly predicting explicit Gaussian scenes. SHARP (Mescheder et al., 2026) and InfiniSplat (Wang et al., 2026b) reconstruct scenes from single image, while GS-LRM (Zhang et al., 2024) combines multiple views. NoPoSplat (Ye et al., 2025) and FLARE (Zhang et al., 2025) support reconstruction without supplied camera poses. Long-LRM (Ziwen et al., 2025) and tttLRM (Wang et al., 2026a) further extend reconstruction to long input sequences. Work on Gaussian representations also explores different ways to organize and predict primitives: C3G (An et al., 2025) and TokenGS (Ren et al., 2026) use learnable queries or tokens, while VolSplat (Wang et al., 2025b) predicts voxel-aligned Gaussians. More directly related to our work is how geometry is estimated and used for Gaussian prediction. pixelSplat (Charatan et al., 2024) establishes cross-view correspondences through epipolar attention, while MVSplat (Chen et al., 2024a) estimates depth using multi-view cost volumes. DepthSplat (Xu et al., 2025b) augments multi-view depth estimation with pretrained monocular depth features. Learned geometric priors also support Gaussian prediction in AnySplat (Jiang et al., 2025), WorldMirror (Liu et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026), and DA3-GS (Lin et al., 2025). Building on such priors, SplatAnything (Anonymous, 2027) scales up training with diverse synthetic and real-world data. QuerySplat (Li et al., 2026) separately decodes geometry and appearance from frozen geometric features. Our work focuses on learning Gaussian attributes from imperfect predicted point clouds to support high-quality novel view rendering. After the initial prediction, learned refinement uses rendering feedback to update the Gaussian scene. G3R (Chen et al., 2024b) and the refinement module of Flux4D (Wang et al., 2026c) use explicit rendering gradients to guide learned updates. ReSplat (Xu et al., 2025a) instead uses feature-space rendering errors without explicit gradient feedback. Our refiner uses input-view rendering gradients to learn updates to Gaussian attributes while keeping centers fixed.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: Overview. Given input images and optional camera conditions, InfiniSplat v2 constructs point cloud from predicted depth maps and corresponding cameras, then learns Gaussian attributes for its points to regulate their rendering contributions. frozen DA3 branch provides the depth and camera estimates, while trainable attribute branch adapts to rendering through image reconstruction supervision  (Fig. 2)  . We then refine the scene attributes using input-view rendering feedback.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Datasets and baselines. We train InfiniSplat v2 on mixture of Hypersim (Roberts et al., 2021), Raw3D (Team, 2026), and ScanNet++ (Yeshwanth et al., 2023), using disjoint scenes for training and validation. We evaluate on six datasets: DL3DV (Ling et al., 2024), ETH3D (Schops et al., 2017), NRGBD (Azinovic et al., 2022), Mip-NeRF 360 (Barron et al., 2022), RealEstate10K (RE10K) (Zhou et al., 2018), and DTU (Aanæs et al., 2016). We compare with tttLRM (Wang et al., 2026a), AnySplat (Jiang et al., 2025), C3G (An et al., 2025), DA3-GS (Lin et al., 2025), DepthSplat (Xu et al., 2025b), QuerySplat (Li et al., 2026), ReSplat (Xu et al., 2025a), TokenGS (Ren et al., 2026), VolSplat (Wang et al., 2025b), and WorldMirror 2.0 (Team et al., 2026). Evaluation protocol. We use {4, 8, 16} input views and four held-out target views per example, with the same view splits for all methods. We evaluate methods separately in poseconditioned and pose-free settings. We use the same trained model for both settings. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: InfiniSplat v2 improves mean LPIPS and DISTS across six datasets in both pose settings. ETH3D and DTU ablations support fixed centers and attribute adaptation under reconstruction supervision. Learned opacity preferentially suppresses geometrically inconsistent points.

sections.content: A.1 DATA AND VIEW SAMPLING Training data and inputs. Both stages sample Hypersim (Roberts et al., 2021), Raw3D (Team, 2026), and ScanNet++ (Yeshwanth et al., 2023) with probabilities of 60%, 10%, and 30%, using disjoint training and validation scenes. Each sample contains four target views and {4, . . . , 12} input views. The processed images longer side is 1022 pixels for 8, 756 for = 9, 10, and 518 for = 11, 12. Target-view sampling. We rank non-input views by decreasing minimum optical-axis angle a(v, C) (Eq. 5), assigning the upper and lower halves to largeand small-angle pools. Each sample selects the large-angle pool with probability 0.7 or the small-angle pool with probability 0.3, then draws four target views uniformly without replacement. The selected pool must contain at least four candidates. Figure 8 shows the sampled angular distributions. Training masks. Target supervision uses visibility masks constructed from GT depth. target pixel must have finite GT depth greater than 106 and pass the supplied validity mask. After backprojection, it is retained if at least one input view places it in front of the camera and within the image bounds, has valid sampled depth, and satisfies zproj dsrc max(τabs, τreldsrc). The w/o variant samples local interpolation views between input views, retaining target supervision and the full models mask construction. Evaluation views. Voxel merging uses side length of 0.004 in the scale-normalized reconstruction frame. Scale alignment and point construction. Camera alignment applies only scale factor, not the full similarity transform. Predicted and GT poses are expressed relative to their respective reference cameras, using the first input view in sorted order. Predicted depths and translations are normalized by snorm > 0 from Eq. 3. Pose-conditioned and pose-free results are reported and ranked separately. In the pose-free setting, reference input cameras are not reconstruction inputs; they only establish the evaluation reference frame and estimate translation scale from input-camera correspondences. The scene is constructed before evaluation-camera alignment and remains unchanged. Target poses define rendering queries without entering the fit. Alignment rescales reference-relative translations only, rather than applying full Sim(3) transform. For methods predicting intrinsics, target focal lengths are the component-wise median of predicted input focal lengths, scaled to the target resolution, with the reference principal point retained. In the pose-conditioned setting, reference input cameras are available for reconstruction and target intrinsics are fixed to GT. Evaluation target RGB is never used for reconstruction or refinement feedback. Metrics and aggregation. We evaluate novel view rendering with PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and DISTS. sections.content: Opacity learning and pruning can suppress unreliable Gaussians, but fixed centers cannot correct severe errors in predicted geometry. Reconstruction quality therefore remains limited by the geometric 20 Figure 13: Large-scale reconstruction on KITTI. Insets show elevated-view renderings at locations AF. prior. Pixel-aligned prediction also produces redundancy not fully removed by voxel merging, while limited input coverage can leave holes in unobserved regions. Future work will explore stronger geometric priors and more compact Gaussian representations, as well as generative models and camera-trajectory design to address limited coverage.
